Patient note:
A 37-year-old man employed as a city sanitation truck operator was sent to the internal-medicine consultation clinic this morning by his occupational health nurse because of escalating breathlessness when hoisting garbage bins and a desire to have all of his chronic conditions reviewed before the busy summer collection schedule begins. He smoked one pack of cigarettes daily from age 16 until quitting three years ago, and over the past decade he has carried a diagnosis of obstructive lung disease based on office spirometry that consistently shows airflow limitation with only modest reversibility after bronchodilator; the most recent tracing performed two weeks ago revealed an FEV1 of 2.1 L (61 % predicted), an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.58, and a diffusion capacity of 62 % predicted. He ordinarily inhales tiotropium 18 µg each morning, uses a budesonide–formoterol dry-powder inhaler two puffs twice daily, and reaches for albuterol roughly three times per week while loading the truck, though he has avoided emergency-department visits and oral corticosteroids for the last eighteen months. Four years ago routine laboratory screening at his union’s mobile clinic disclosed fasting plasma glucose of 142 mg/dL on two occasions; since then he has taken metformin 1 g twice daily, eats lower-carbohydrate meals packed by his spouse, and logs home glucometer readings that range 110–155 mg/dL before dinner. A hemoglobin A1c drawn last month was 7.2 %, he confirms intact light-touch sensation in the soles, and his last dilated retinal examination was normal, with no proteinuria on a spot urine sample. He denies crushing substernal pressure, radiating arm pain, diaphoresis out of proportion to exertion, syncope, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, or ankle swelling; participation in a neighborhood softball league allows him to jog the bases without chest tightness, and a screening resting echocardiogram obtained by an urgent-care clinic after a viral upper-respiratory illness nine months ago demonstrated normal chamber sizes, preserved systolic function, and no valvular abnormality. He has never been told he suffered a heart attack, has not undergone coronary catheterization, and serial high-sensitivity troponins drawn during two separate emergency evaluations for pleuritic chest discomfort related to bronchitis were undetectable. Neurologic review is negative for transient unilateral weakness, facial droop, speech disturbance, monocular vision loss, or gait imbalance, and he balances the household budget on a spreadsheet without lapses in short-term memory. He reports no calf cramping when climbing the steps of his truck, no discoloration of toes, and pedal pulses were documented as palpable by his primary practitioner last autumn. Two years ago a comprehensive metabolic panel showed alanine aminotransferase 58 U/L and aspartate aminotransferase 49 U/L; an abdominal ultrasound demonstrated homogeneous increased echogenicity consistent with hepatic steatosis but smooth contour, patent portal and hepatic veins, and no splenomegaly. Follow-up laboratories drawn yesterday remain similar—ALT 56 U/L, AST 47 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 72 U/L, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, albumin 4.2 g/dL, and international normalized ratio 1.0—and he denies abdominal distention, jaundice, pruritus, easy bruising, hematemesis, or melena. Renal indices are normal with sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, chloride 103 mmol/L, bicarbonate 25 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 14 mg/dL, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, and an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 105 mL/min/1.73 m². Lipid profile shows total cholesterol 196 mg/dL, LDL 118 mg/dL, HDL 46 mg/dL, and triglycerides 140 mg/dL; he takes atorvastatin 20 mg nightly without myalgias. He drinks two bottles of light beer on Saturday evenings, has never used illicit substances, and reports no allergies. Family history is notable for a father with type 2 diabetes diagnosed in his fifties and a mother with asthma; no first-degree relatives experienced myocardial infarction or stroke before age 65. Vital signs today: temperature 36.9 °C, blood pressure 128/78 mm Hg seated in the right arm, pulse 86 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 95 % breathing ambient air, and body-mass index 31 kg/m². He sits comfortably yet occasionally pauses midsentence to take a deeper breath. Oropharynx is clear, neck supple with no lymphadenopathy, carotid upstrokes are brisk without bruit, and jugular venous pulsation is 4 cm above the sternal angle at 45°. The cardiac point of maximal impulse is at the fifth intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line; S1 and S2 are audible with physiologic splitting, no murmurs, rubs, or gallops are detected. Breath sounds reveal scattered end-expiratory wheezes and prolonged expiration bilaterally without crackles. Abdomen is soft and non-tender; the liver edge is smooth, 1 cm below the right costal margin, and ascites is absent. Extremities are warm with 2+ radial, femoral, dorsalis pedis, and posterior tibial pulses, no edema or stasis changes, and capillary refill under two seconds. Neurologic examination shows orientation to person, place, and time, intact cranial nerves II–XII, 5/5 strength throughout, symmetric reflexes, normal sensation, and steady tandem gait. A portable chest radiograph obtained in clinic depicts hyperinflated lungs with flattened diaphragms, clear parenchyma, and a normal cardiac silhouette. Twelve-lead electrocardiogram reveals normal sinus rhythm at 84 beats/min with no pathologic Q waves, ST-segment deviation, or conduction delay. He requests optimization of breathing medications before warmer weather, guidance on adjusting metformin doses when meal schedules vary during double shifts, and counseling on weight-loss strategies that will not exacerbate his liver enzyme elevations or jeopardize his ability to climb aboard the truck cab.

Question: What is the patient's Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) sums weighted comorbidities; age adjustment adds no points before age 50.
1. Age 37 → 0.
2. Chronic pulmonary disease: persistent airflow obstruction (FEV1/FVC 0.58) requiring maintenance inhalers → 1.
3. Diabetes without end-organ damage: metformin-treated diabetes with no documented neuropathy, retinopathy, or nephropathy → 1.
4. Mild liver disease: hepatic steatosis with persistent mild transaminase elevation, preserved synthetic function, and no evidence of portal hypertension → 1.
5. No other qualifying comorbidity is documented → 0.
Total: 0 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 0 = 3.
Final answer: 3
